title: Those We Carry in Our Hearts
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Kurt Wootton, writing from Yucatan, describes how his children's school folds Dia de los Muertos into its culture, including a Noche Mexicana evening with altars, a parade and music. The piece centers on an exhibit created by the Spanish department, Versos para quienes llevamos en el corazon, in which each student brought a photograph of a person or pet to honor and wrote a poem to accompany it. Each photograph carried a QR code linking to the student reading the poem aloud, and Wootton's son honored the family dog, Fluffy. He notes the layers of community in the room: students connecting with those who had died, parents hearing what their children felt, and families sharing recordings with relatives abroad. Citing a New York Times description of the holiday as a shared ritual of remembrance, he argues that schools too often turn away from difficult topics. Writing for a specific purpose and audience, he concludes, lifts a classroom beyond routine and makes extraordinary things possible.
points: A school exhibition tied to a cultural ritual can turn a language assignment into a community event with real emotional weight.
Writing for a specific purpose and audience, here poems honoring someone loved, gives student work meaning beyond a grade.
Pairing photographs with QR-linked recordings let families far away take part, extending the audience for student writing.
Schools gain by engaging difficult subjects such as loss and memory rather than avoiding them.
quotes: I find it beautiful that once a year, we can welcome those we have lost back into our homes, even if only for a brief visit.

It’s not surprising, then, that Día de los Muertos is incorporated into school culture here. My children's school holds an evening celebration with altars set up around the campus, a parade, music, and other festivities.
Each photograph had a QR code linking to a recording of the student reading a poem they had written to honor the person or animal they “carried in their heart.

At the exhibit, parents were photographing their children’s work and sending the students’ readings of their poems to relatives around the world. What struck me were the layers of community present in the room.
Students were connecting with someone who had passed away. Parents were hearing their children express how much a person or pet had meant to them.

Often we turn away from these difficult topics in schools. It is precisely this kind of meaningful work—writing for a specific purpose and audience—that lifts a classroom beyond the routines of everyday school life
